take: Brent’s slide to $85 is the day’s key story, with the Iran-Oman plan for a temporary Hormuz maritime corridor directly deflating the geopolitical risk premium that had underpinned crude and product cracks. The shift in tanker flows is the second theme, as Aramco’s move to offer more September cargoes via ship-to-ship handoffs signals a structural workaround that will distort VLCC tonne-mile demand and regional freight differentials even if the strait reopens. Positioning is clearly long and crowded, evidenced by the three-session drop in Brent as longs liquidate on the mine-clearance headlines, whilst the market ignores Iran’s retaliation threats against US sanctions. The cross-market link is tight: a functioning Hormuz corridor normalises bunker fuel availability in Fujairah and Singapore, pressuring HSFO-VLSFO spreads, whilst Nigerian product exports, up seven-fold since 2023, continue to weigh on Atlantic basin clean product freight. Watch for any official confirmation of the Hormuz corridor framework’s implementation timeline, plus the next EIA inventory print to gauge whether the US Gulf Coast-to-West Coast waiver-driven surge in waterborne shipments persists.

items.title: Waterborne shipments from the U.S. Gulf Coast increased in April and May

Shipments from the U.S. Gulf Coast to the East Coast (PADD 1) also increased.
